chunks: My father, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Ahmad ibn Idris narrated to us, from al-Husayn ibn Abdullah, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from one of the people of al-Mada'in, who said: I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him): It has been narrated to us from your fathers (peace be upon them) that your narration is difficult and complicated, which a close angel does not endure, nor a sent prophet, nor a believer whose heart Allah has tested for faith. He said: The answer came to him: Its meaning is that the angel does not endure it in his chest until he brings it out to an angel like himself, nor does a prophet endure it until he brings it out to a prophet like himself, nor does a believer endure it until he brings it out to a believer like himself. Its meaning is that it is not endured in the heart from the sweetness of what is in one's chest until one brings it out to someone else.

key_terms.حُلْوَةُ: Sweetness (metaphor for the delight of knowledge)
key_terms.صَدْرٌ: Chest (metaphor for the heart/mind containing knowledge)
key_terms.مُسْتَصْعَبٌ: Difficult and complicated / hard to endure
key_terms.نَبِيٌّ مُرْسَلٌ: Sent prophet with a divine message

ai.seo_question: Why do the Imams say their hadiths are difficult to bear?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this clarification from Imam al-Hadi (AS) to resolve the apparent paradox of the Imams' 'difficulty' in bearing their own narrations. He interprets the 'weight' not as a burden of comprehension, but as the preciousness of the divine sweetness (halaawah) that prevents the Imam from parting with it until it is transmitted to an equal successor, emphasizing the exclusivity and high status of Ahl al-Bayt knowledge. This highlights the concept of 'taqlid' and the spiritual hierarchy where knowledge is a sacred trust passed from master to worthy disciple.
